chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter opens with the queen's locker puzzle and lets the answer, the square numbers, lead into everything else. Each idea starts with a prediction (will this locker stay open, can a square end in 7, how many cubes make this block), then a picture or a pattern explains why. Squares come first, as areas, digits and sums of odd numbers; then square roots by three methods and by estimation; then the same journey for cubes.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Every concept opens with a question the student answers before the video reveals it, such as which lockers stay open or whether 2032 can be a square.

points.title: Pictures that prove
points.text: Squares are drawn as tiles and cubes as stacks of unit cubes, and the odd number pattern is shown with inverted L shapes, so each rule is seen before it is used.

points.title: One tool, one idea
points.text: Ten tools, each used once, appear only where handling the objects is the idea itself: lockers and squares, building squares and cubes, odd-number corners, the gap between squares, finding a side from an area, pairing and tripling prime factors, trapping a root between two whole numbers, and a ladder of differences.

points.title: Several roads to a root
points.text: Square roots are found by listing squares, by subtracting odd numbers, by pairing prime factors and by estimating with nearby squares, and the student learns when each road is quickest.

concepts.concept_name: A hundred lockers and a hidden treasure

content.text:
Queen Ratnamanjuri of Khoisnam left a will. Her treasure was kept in one of the 100 lockers in her palace, all closed and locked.
100 people were called one after another. The first person opened every locker. The second person closed every second locker: locker 2, 4, 6, and so on. The third person toggled every third locker: if it was open it was closed, and if it was closed it was opened. The fourth person toggled every fourth locker, and so on, until the hundredth person toggled locker 100.
After all 100 people had done this, which lockers remain open?
Hint: Find the number of times each locker is toggled.

content.text:
1. Predict first: after all 100 people have passed, do you think most lockers end open, most end closed, or only a few end open?
2. Try a small case by hand: 10 lockers and 10 people. Keep a record of which lockers each person touches.
3. A locker that is touched an odd number of times ends open; an even number of times, closed.
4. So the real question is: how many times is each locker touched? Keep that question open for the next topic.

content.text:
Worked example: How many times is locker 12 toggled, and does it end open or closed?
1. Locker 12 is toggled by every person whose number divides 12.
2. The factors of 12 pair up: 12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4.
3. That is 6 factors, so locker 12 is toggled 6 times.
4. An even number of toggles brings it back to closed.
Answer: 6 times, so locker 12 ends closed

concepts.concept_name: Squares have an odd number of factors

content.text:
Can you use this insight to find more numbers with an odd number of factors?
For 36: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6. The factor 6 is paired with itself.
Numbers like 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 4 × 4 are called square numbers.
Square numbers have an odd number of factors.

concepts.concept_name: A square number is an area

content.text:
1.1 Square Numbers
The area of a square of side 1 unit is 1 sq unit, of side 2 units is 4 sq units, of side 3 units is 9 sq units. For sides 4, 5 and 10 the areas are 16, 25 and 100 sq units.
A square of side n units has area n × n = n² sq units, read as n squared.
We can square fractions and decimals too: (3/5)² = 9/25 and 2.5² = 6.25.
Numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 which are squares of natural numbers are called perfect squares.

4. Squares of natural numbers, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, are called perfect squares.

content.text:
Fill in the table of squares from 1 to 30.
What patterns do you notice? The squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
If a number ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, is it always a square? No: 26 ends in 6 but is not a square.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a perfect square end in 7?
2. Only the last digit of a number decides the last digit of its square. Squaring 0 to 9 gives last digits 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1.
3. So squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a square.
4. The converse fails: 26 ends in 6 but is not a square. A last digit can rule a square out, never in.
5. A number ending in 4 or 6 has a square ending in 6; ending in 1 or 9, a square ending in 1.

2. 3000² = 3000 × 3000. Each factor brings 3 zeros, so the square ends in 6 zeros: 9000000.
3. The zeros double, so a perfect square always ends in an even number of zeros.
4. Odd times odd is odd and even times even is even, so a number and its square have the same parity.

media.title: Square Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, A Square and A Cube, the opening of the square. NCERT Ganita Prakash builds squares on a DOT GRID and the older NCERT builds them as unit-square AREA; this tool reads the grid as unit tiles, which is legible in both. It sits BEFORE the square root is introduced in this same chapter, so the radical sign never appears and the reverse direction is asked as 'what is its side?', never as 'find the root'. Products are written with U+00D7. The chapter's own odd-number-sum pattern (1, 1+3, 1+3+5) IS the L-shaped border arithmetically, and the tool names them as the same fact.

overview.goal: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground, the way squared paper sits on a desk, with the tile array as the only object on it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class argues that seven squared is fourteen, and the square itself is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A square of side n is an n by n array of unit tiles, so it holds n times n tiles. That count is written n squared. Because the figure is a square, width always equals height, so one number n fixes the whole picture and the tile count follows from it.
overview.purpose: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Square fills the main panel with the side readout above it and the tile count directly beneath. The n and n squared table sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses to a single scrolling strip under the square on a 390 px frame. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the tile count, the table or the rule while a prediction is still open. The count IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Filling the square row by row gives n rows of n tiles, which is n added to itself n times, that is n times n. Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds an L shaped border of two arms of n and one corner tile, so the count grows by 2n plus 1 and never by a fixed amount, which is exactly why doubling cannot be the rule. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

media.description: A square of unit tiles stands on a plain working ground with one drag handle that moves its width and its height together, so a single number n fixes the whole picture. The array fills one row at a time from the bottom, the count climbing by a whole row rather than by a tile, and a running table of n against n squared builds beside it on a wide pane. Stepping the side up by one lights the added L shaped border in a second colour, drawn as three separately counted pieces - an arm of n, a second arm of n, and one corner tile that lands last - so 2n + 1 is watched rather than asserted, and the same number is named as the next odd number, which is the textbook's own explanation of the growth. A claimed count that cannot be a square is drawn as tiles that RUN OUT inside the ruled grid, with a bracket strip placing it between the two whole sides that bracket it, so the doubling error is refuted by a picture of an unfinishable square rather than by a red cross. Above side 12 the tiles stop being drawn and the square becomes a labelled outline carrying its count, which is where the rule has to take over from counting. A typed rule is parsed to a small expression tree - never eval - and run against the tool's own ground truth at n equal to 5, 9 and 25, with every disagreeing row washed in the second colour, because agreement at a single value is not a rule.

modes.ai: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a 4 by 4 grid with the tile count HIDDEN and asks the class to predict how many small tiles a side of 7 will hold. Beat 2 fills the square one row at a time and the count lands beside the guess. Beat 3 steps the side up once and lights the added L shaped border in the second colour, so what each step adds is watchable before anyone writes a rule. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, fillRows, highlightLShape and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.
modes.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the side from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the filled square, the running n and n squared table and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
modes.normal: Free Play, student operated. The student drags the side from 1 to 12, fills and empties the square, shows or hides the n and n squared table, and tests any rule they like against fresh values of n. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.
modes.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own square. Give the tile count for a stated side, give the side for a stated count, or type a rule for any side n. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the square that settles it.

concept.notation: Write n squared, read as 'n squared' or 'n to the power 2'. The raised 2 counts how many factors of n are multiplied, it is not a multiplier.
concept.statement: A square of side n is an n by n array of unit tiles, so it holds n times n tiles. That count is written n squared. Because the figure is a square, width always equals height, so one number n fixes the whole picture and the tile count follows from it.
prerequisites: area of a rectangle as length times breadth from Class 7
misconceptions: Squaring read as doubling, so 7 squared is taken as 14. The array makes 14 impossible to draw as a square.
Reading the raised 2 as 'times 2' rather than as a count of equal factors.
concept.why_it_is_true: Filling the square row by row gives n rows of n tiles, which is n added to itself n times, that is n times n. Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds an L shaped border of two arms of n and one corner tile, so the count grows by 2n plus 1 and never by a fixed amount, which is exactly why doubling cannot be the rule.
worked_numbers: side 4 gives 4 rows of 4, so 16 tiles; doubling would have said 8.
side 7 gives 49 tiles; the doubling answer 14 is smaller than one row of the square plus its neighbour.
side 12 gives 144 tiles, the largest square the grid draws before it switches to an outline.

answer_key.worked: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared. The count is the area of the square in unit tiles.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn square: the tile count for the stated side, the side for the stated count, or whether the typed rule agrees with n squared at every tested n.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only. No floating point value decides a tile count or a side, and no rule is graded by string comparison.
answer_key.ground_truth: tiles(n) = n * n, computed as an integer product. side(t) = the integer s with s*s === t, found by integer search, or null when no such s exists. ruleAgrees(text) = parse the typed rule to a small expression tree and evaluate it at n = 5, 9 and 25, comparing each value with n*n.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: A single tile. It is a legal square and the smallest one, and the table starts at 1 and 1 so the student sees that squaring leaves 1 unmoved. Never treat it as an empty scene.

constraints: The figure stays a square at every moment: width always equals height, and a drag that would separate them is refused rather than corrected silently.
Tiles stay whole and non overlapping. No partial tile is ever drawn to make a count come out.
The tile count is computed as an integer product n * n, never accumulated by counting rendered rects, so a redraw cannot drift.
Render is capped at 144 tiles. Above a side of 12 the square switches to a labelled outline and the tool says the tiles are not drawn.
A typed rule is parsed to a small expression tree and evaluated numerically, never passed to eval, so 2n plus 1 style input is safe and n times n and n squared both pass.

visual_behaviour.scene: A square array of unit tiles on a plain ground, one drag handle on the right side and one on the bottom moving together. Filled tiles carry the primary accent; the L shaped border added by the last step carries the second accent; the outline stays a thin uniform stroke.

animations: Row fill: each row of tiles fades in left to right over 180 ms, staggered 60 ms per row, so the count reads as n groups of n rather than as a block appearing.
L shaped border: on a step up the two arms sweep out from the corner and the single corner tile lands last with one pulse, which is the moment 2n plus 1 becomes visible.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the count is SEEN arriving as seven groups of seven rather than as a block appearing. The array fills a row at a time and the count climbs by a whole row, which is what makes n squared a multiplication instead of an addition. Do not write the rule down at this beat; it is the count that is being made.

Beat 2 is the refutation, and it works because 14 is EXACTLY two rows of seven. The fourteen tiles fill two complete rows and then stop, with five rows of the ruled grid still empty, so the doubling answer is not merely wrong on paper - it is an unfinishable square. The bracket strip then shows 14 sitting between 9 and 16, which is why no whole side gives it at all.

Beat 3 turns the observation into a rule the class can test. The added border arrives as three separately counted pieces and the corner tile lands LAST, so a student who said '+1' watches fifteen tiles land and a student who said '+7' sees the second arm and the corner arrive after their answer was complete. The second chip carries 9 to 10 adding 19, because one step teaches nothing here and two do: the step GROWS, which is precisely why doubling cannot be the rule.

content.text:
Perfect Squares and Odd Numbers
Look at the differences between consecutive squares: 4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7, 25 − 16 = 9. See if this pattern continues.
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36.
Each square is the previous square with an inverted L shape added to it. The inverted L shapes have 1, 3, 5, 7, ... dots. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².
Such pictures are visual proofs.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the differences between consecutive squares, recognise them as the odd numbers, and explain with the inverted L picture why the first n odd numbers add to n squared.
Students subtract 1, 3, 5 and so on from a number in turn and decide it is a perfect square exactly when the subtractions reach 0, counting the steps to find the root.
Students find the nth odd number as 2n − 1 and use it to get the next square from a given square.
Students use the odd number pattern to get squares from neighbouring squares and to check number patterns built from squares.

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 8): Look at the pattern 1² + 2² + 2² = 3², 2² + 3² + 6² = 7², 3² + 4² + 12² = 13². Fill in 4² + 5² + 20² = (___)² and 9² + 10² + (___)² = (___)².
1. In each line the third number is the product of the first two: 1 × 2 = 2, 2 × 3 = 6, 3 × 4 = 12.
2. The number on the right is one more than that product: 3, 7, 13.
3. 4 × 5 = 20, so 4² + 5² + 20² = 21². Check: 16 + 25 + 400 = 441 = 21².
4. 9 × 10 = 90, so 9² + 10² + 90² = 91². Check: 81 + 100 + 8100 = 8281 = 91².
Answer: 4² + 5² + 20² = 21² and 9² + 10² + 90² = 91²
